span.label: existence
span.quote: Using six historical corpora spanning four languages and two centuries, we propose two quantitative laws of semantic change: (i) the law of conformity—the rate of semantic change scales with an inverse power-law of word frequency; (ii) the law of innovation—independent of frequency, words that are more polysemous have higher rates of semantic change.

span.label: semantic change
span.quote: Understanding how words change their meanings over time is key to models of language and cultural evolution, but historical data on meaning is scarce, making theories hard to develop and test.

span.quote: We then apply this methodology in a large-scale cross-linguistic analysis using 6 corpora spanning 200 years and 4 languages (English, German, French, and Chinese).

span.label: The paper's results are correlational; it explicitly declines to claim the causal mechanisms it speculates about.
span.quote: While our results cannot confirm such causal links, they nonetheless highlight a new role for frequency and polysemy in language change and the importance of distributional models in historical research.

span.label: The polysemy proxy (local clustering coefficient in a PPMI co-occurrence network) is biased towards rating contextually diverse function words as highly polysemous.
span.quote: However, we found that it was slightly biased towards rating contextually diverse discourse function words (e.g., also) as highly polysemous, which needs to be taken into account when interpreting our results.

span.label: Polysemy has no agreed ground truth to validate the measure against.
span.quote: Measuring word polysemy is a difficult and fraught task, as even “ground truth” dictionaries differ in the number of senses they assign to words (Simpson et al., 1989; Fellbaum, 1998).

span.label: The main corpora contain artifacts from shifting sampling biases over time.
span.quote: The Google N-Gram datasets are extremely large (comprising≈6% of all books ever published), but they also contain many corpus artifacts due, e.g., to shifting sampling biases over time (Pechenick et al., 2015).
